book.title: Mahmud Kashgari and His Work Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk

pages.title: The First Linguistic Study of Turkic
pages.content:
Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk, which literally means ‘Dictionary of Turkic Dialects,’ is the first linguistic study of the Turkic language. It was written by Mahmud Kashgari in the 11th century and records Karakhanid Turkic. A dialect is a regional form of a language with its own unique vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation. So, as the title of the work suggests, this study includes the speech patterns, vocabulary, and grammatical structures of various Turkic tribes.

Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk was compiled as a dictionary from Turkic dialects to Arabic. This monumental work aims to teach the Turkic language to Arabs while demonstrating that its richness is comparable to Arabic. The comprehensive content of the work reflects that Mahmud Kashgari had a very good command of both Arabic and Persian, as well as knowledge of the dictionaries written in these languages.

pages.title: Writing the Dîvân
pages.content: Mahmud Kashgari began writing Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk in 1072 and, after revising it several times and making new additions, completed it in 1074. Subsequently, he presented his work to the Abbasid Caliph Muktedî-Biemrillâh in Baghdad in 1077. To the present day, the full text of Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk has been translated into Turkish, Uzbek, Kazakh, Modern Uyghur, English, Chinese, Persian, and Azerbaijani. The work contains approximately 9,000 Turkic words, proverbs, and idioms. It also contains the oldest examples of Turkic poetry, the grammar rules of the Turkic language, numerous place names, personal names, and various traditions, beliefs, and legends from the Turkic world of that era. It also includes information and practices related to nearly every aspect of life. From this perspective, the work can be regarded as an encyclopedia of Turkic culture.

pages.title: Who Was Mahmud Kashgari?
pages.content:
Kashgari is considered to have been born in 1008 and to have died in 1105. It is generally accepted that he was born in Barsgan, which is within the borders of present-day Kyrgyzstan, and died in Kashgar. Kashgar is located today within China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, an ancient Turkish homeland also widely known as East Turkestan.

Kashgari says that his forefather was Nasr Ilig Khan (Ebu’l Hüseyin Nasr) of the Karakhanids, the conqueror of Transoxiana and Bukhara. He describes himself as “one of the Turks who know the language best, one of the most eloquent in expression, one of the wisest, one of the most distinguished in ancestry, and one of the best spear throwers.” In fact, his father was a member of the Karakhanid ruling class. He also took lessons from the leading scholars of his time. Among the subjects he studied under various scholars were the Qur’an, Hadith, Tafsir, Fiqh, Arabic, Persian, linguistics, literature, Ilm-i Hesap (mathematics), algebra, Hendese (geometry), physics, chemistry, Ilm-i Coğrafya (geography), and Ilm-i Tebabet (medicine).

pages.title: In His Own Words
pages.content:
“Allah Himself named them (the Turks) and placed them in the highest region of the earth, where the air is the purest. He declared them as His own, saying, ‘They are My army.’ The Turks also have many admirable qualities worthy of praise, such as beauty, charm, bright faces, good manners, respect for elders, loyalty to one’s word, modesty, and bravery.”

He adds the following about the Turks and the Turkic language: “I saw that Allah made the sun of the kingdom rise in the tower of the Turks and made all the heavens revolve under their dominion. He gave them the name ‘Turk,’ made them rulers, and established them as the dominant power of the age. He placed the governance of the people of that age in their hands, set them at the head of the people, and supported them on the path of righteousness. He honors those who follow them and walk in their ways, grants them whatever they desire, and protects them from the oppression of wicked people. [Then I realized that] what fits a person of reason is to follow the path that these people have taken in order to protect oneself from becoming a target of their arrows. To make one’s voice heard and to win their hearts, there is no better way than to speak in their language. When an enemy, out of fear, comes to seek refuge with them, they keep him safe. Then another seeks refuge with him, and the harm is removed.”

pages.title: The Hadith and the Journey
pages.content: He also records the following hadith. Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) says, “Learn the Turkish language! This is because the Turks will have a long-lasting kingdom.” It was with this belief and confidence that he set out on his journey and began his tours of all Turkic countries. Mahmud of Kashgar left his homeland in 1057. During the ten to fifteen years that followed, until he reached Baghdad, he traveled from one Turkic tribe to another and gathered the material that he needed for his work. He states that he studied the lands of the Turks, that he learned the dialects of the Turks, Turkmen, Oghuz, Chigil, Yagma, and Kyrgyz, and that he knew the speech of every tribe perfectly.

pages.title: The Oghuz and the Caliph
pages.content: The Oghuz are the Turkic tribe that receives the most attention in the work, both in terms of vocabulary and other aspects, and a great deal of information is provided about them. At that time, the Oghuz were the dominant group in the western part of the Turkic world, in the Arab and Persian regions. The information that Kashgari gives about the Oghuz is not limited to their languages. He also provides quite valuable explanations regarding their tribal organization. He records the names of twenty-two out of the twenty-four Oghuz tribes. The likely reason for this is that, in addition to their strong influence, the Seljuks, an Oghuz Turkic tribe, had taken the Abbasids, the center of the Islamic caliphate, under their protection. The fact that a work with such content was completed in Baghdad and presented to the caliph holds special significance. Kashgari was likely aware of both the political power of the three great Turkic states, namely the Karakhanids, the Ghaznavids, and the Seljuks, and the fact that the caliphate was protected by the Turks.

pages.title: Why Turkish?
pages.content: In the madrasas of the Karakhanid and Transoxiana cultural centers, Arabic was the primary language of instruction. The scholars of the era also wrote their works in Arabic. It is likely that Arabic’s dominant status inspired Kashgari to praise his native language, Turkish. In the face of Arabic’s dominance, Kashgari wrote Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk, driven by a belief in the greatness of his mother tongue and its ability to rival Arabic.

pages.title: The Importance of the Map
pages.content:
In addition to all this linguistic material, the book also contains a map of the Turkic world of his time. Mahmud of Kashgar not only described the geography inhabited by the Turkic tribes but also pointed out the regions inhabited by Turkic peoples on the map he included in his work, noting that “each of these tribes is shown on this map.” Owing to this map, Kashgari is widely recognized as the first Turkic cartographer.

The map features a multicolored, circular design. It illustrates mountains in red, seas in green, rivers in blue, and sandy areas in yellow, while also displaying the nations that interacted with the Turks. Mahmud of Kashgar states that Allah placed the Turks on the highest mountains, the center of the world, to enable them to rule the earth and hold authority over all four corners of the earth. It is likely that he designed his map to reflect this belief. On the map, Turkestan, the homeland of the Turks, is placed at the center of the world, and the city of Balasagun, located in modern-day Kyrgyzstan, is positioned right in the heart of it. In fact, Balasagun was located on a highly active part of the Silk Road. All other countries, cities, and mountains are placed according to this center. This map is considered the oldest document created from a Turkic geographical perspective.

According to modern geography, the locations and illustrations on Mahmud of Kashgar’s world map extend to the Russian border and the Idil (Volga) River in the west. In the south, they stretch from the Egyptian border to Ethiopia and India, reaching China and Japan in the east. Notably, Japan is identified on the map as ‘Jabarqa,’ while China is referred to as ‘the Land of Yecüc and Mecüc.’

Based on what we know today, the map in Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is the first world map to depict Japan. The second world map to show Japan was created about four centuries after his work. This demonstrates the importance of the document once again.

pages.title: The Story of the Calendar
pages.content:
The book also mentions the ancient calendar used by the Turks. In the dictionary section of the book, Kashgari describes in detail the characteristics of the Twelve-Animal Turkic calendar, how it emerged, and its role in the lives of the Turks. He mentions that the Turks created a twelve-year calendar by giving the names of twelve different animals to the years. He notes that they used this system to record their children’s ages, the dates of battles, and other events. He describes the interesting story of this calendar as follows:

One of the Turkic khans (a title used by Turkish rulers since the pre-Islamic period) wished to learn about a battle from earlier times, prior to his own reign. When those around him disagreed on the date of this battle, the khan gathered a kurultay (national meeting, general meeting) and consulted his people.

“If we are mistaken about this date, those who come after us will also be mistaken. To prevent this, let us establish a system based on the twelve stars of the sky and the twelve months. Let us give each year a name. In this way, we will determine time by counting these years. Let this system serve as a record for all of us,” he said.

The people also approved of the khan’s idea. They determined the names to be given to the years as follows:

The khan went out hunting and ordered the people to drive the wild animals toward a large river in the Ili Valley. The Ili Valley is a historically and geographically significant region located in the northern part of East Turkestan, stretching across the border into Kazakhstan. The people drove them toward the river. Only twelve animals managed to cross the river. Starting with the first animal to cross, the rat, the name of each subsequent animal was given to the following years. Thus, the calendar begins with the Year of the Rat. Following the rat, the years in the twelve-animal Turkish calendar are determined according to the animals that crossed the river in the order listed below:

pages.title: What Each Year Means
pages.content:
In the Twelve-Animal Turkic calendar, some years are considered prosperous, while others are considered tough. So, the Turks have a belief for each year and derive certain meanings from it. If it is the Year of the Ox, they say that wars will increase because the ox is known for butting. When the Year of the Rooster begins, food becomes more abundant, but disorder spreads among people because the rooster’s food is grain, and it constantly scratches through the garbage dump. When the Year of the Snake and the Year of the Crocodile begin, there is rain and fertility because these animals’ natural habitat is water. When the Year of the Pig begins, cold, snow, and disorder increase. In this way, they make different predictions for each year.

After the Year of the Pig, the cycle resets and returns to the Year of the Rat, and the dating continues.

According to this calendar, the Earth’s age is 3,600,000 years. A cycle lasts 12 years. A year consists of 365 days and a little over 5 hours. One year consists of 12 months. One month consists of 30 days. The day begins at midnight. The seven days of the week have no names. A day is divided into twelve parts, meaning each period lasts two hours under this system. This two-hour period is called a “çağ.”

pages.title: Orkhon Inscriptions and Nowruz
pages.content:
It is known that this calendar was used by the Turks for a long time. In the Orkhon Inscriptions, erected in the years 725, 731, and 732, that is, centuries before Kashgari began writing his Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk, historical events are described according to the Twelve-Animal Turkic calendar. The names of the months are given as ‘birinç ay’ for the first month and ‘bişinç ay’ for the fifth month.

Based on information provided by Kashgari, the Turks’ twelve-animal calendar begins on March 21 in the calendar we use today. Nowruz, which the Turks have celebrated since the earliest times, marks the beginning of the new year according to the twelve-animal Turkish calendar. Today, Turks and various communities in the Turkic world and in our region continue to celebrate Nowruz.

vocabulary.definition: Built or put up.
Shows the start of something.

pages.title: Excerpts from the Dîvân
pages.content:
To give a better idea of the work’s content, here are a few excerpts from Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk. These pieces will also allow us to compare the Turkish of that period with the modern form.

The word alp: An “alp” is brave. As the proverb goes, “Alp yagıda alçak çogıda,” which means, “A hero is tested in battle against the enemy. A person of quiet character is tested in an argument.”

The word “öz” is explained as follows: it means “self.” They say:

Körklüg tonug özünke

Tatlıg aşıg adınka

Tutgıl konuk agırlıg

Yadsun çavın bodunka

Meaning: Wear the beautiful clothes yourself. Let others enjoy the delicious food. Entertain the guest, so that these things may spread your reputation among the people.

vocabulary.definition: Short parts taken from a longer text.
The opinion that people have about someone.

languageFocusExercises.title: Use: Interpret a Proverb
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write a paragraph of six to eight sentences interpreting a proverb from your culture.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does it mean, and is it still true today?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Example: “As the proverb goes, ‘Komşu komşunun külüne muhtaçtır,’ which means that neighbors need each other even for the smallest things. The proverb comes from a time when people borrowed fire and ash from each other. Like the poem in the Dîvân, it values sharing. Today, many people in cities do not know their neighbors. However, during earthquakes and snowstorms, neighbors are often the first to help. The proverb is still true, and it reminds us to greet our neighbors so that no one may feel alone.”

pages.title: Founder of Turkic Studies
pages.content: Mahmud of Kashgar is regarded as an exceptionally well-educated linguist. The work he wrote has gained him the title of founder of Turkic studies. At Turkey’s suggestion and with the support of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan, the 950th Anniversary of the Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk has been included in UNESCO’s 2024 Program of Anniversaries to Be Commemorated and Celebrated. Today, the only surviving copy of Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk, which dates back to the year 1266, is kept at the Millet Library in Istanbul.

Remembered with a special event.
A copy that still exists today.
Was made at a time in the past.

languageFocusExercises.title: Use: Arguing for Heritage
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write an argument of eight to ten sentences about why a cultural work deserves international recognition.
languageFocusExercises.question: Why should the world remember it?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Example: “Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk, whose only surviving copy dates back to 1266, deserves international recognition. First, it has gained its author the title of founder of Turkic studies. Second, it has been translated into many languages, so scholars around the world can study it. It also contains a map that is the first to depict Japan. Some may argue that an old dictionary interests only linguists. However, its proverbs, poems and calendar tell us about the daily life and values of a whole civilization. For this reason, its inclusion in UNESCO’s 2024 program was well deserved. Recognizing such works helps different countries share a common heritage.”

feedback.correct: Check: a non-defining clause, the present perfect, a counterpoint and a conclusion.

discussionPrompts.question: Introduce the work with a non-defining clause and date back to.
Give two reasons with the present perfect.

exercises.title: Notice: How Certain Is the Writer?
exercises.instructions: Sort the sentences: presented as known fact, or as accepted, considered or likely?
exercises.question: How certain is the writer?

items: Mahmud of Kashgar left his homeland in 1057.
It is known that this calendar was used by the Turks for a long time.
Kashgari is considered to have been born in 1008.
It is likely that he designed his map to reflect this belief.

Known fact: Mahmud of Kashgar left his homeland in 1057.
It is known that this calendar was used by the Turks for a long time.
Accepted, considered or likely: Kashgari is considered to have been born in 1008.
It is likely that he designed his map to reflect this belief.

exercises.explanation: The writer signals certainty with It is known that and hedges with is considered to, It is generally accepted that and It is likely that (Chapters 3, 5, 8 and 12).

feedback.correct: Good. You noticed the degrees of certainty.
feedback.incorrect: Look for known, considered and likely.

It not only contains poems but also it contains a map.

exercises.explanation: Use the present perfect with since, the perfect passive infinitive for a past event, and parallel forms after not only … but also.

exercises.title: Use: Language, Memory and Identity
exercises.instructions: Write an argument of eight to ten sentences: why do communities record their languages and traditions?
exercises.question: Use evidence from the book and one counterpoint.
exercises.explanation: Example: “Communities record their languages and traditions because these records keep their memory alive. For example, Kashgari collected the dialects of many tribes and recorded about 9,000 words, proverbs and idioms (Chapters 2 and 5). His excerpts allow us to compare Old Turkic with modern Turkish (Chapter 13). In addition, the Orkhon Inscriptions show that the Twelve-Animal calendar was used centuries before him (Chapter 12). Some may argue that old words are no longer useful in a modern world. However, without such records, we could not understand how our language and values developed. It is likely that future generations will value our records in the same way. Therefore, recording a language is an act of responsibility toward the future.”

feedback.correct: Check: a clear position, evidence from two chapters, a counterpoint and a conclusion.

Give evidence from at least two chapters.
Consider a counterpoint and conclude.
